documents.title: Authentication overview
documents.text: Every call to the Meridian API carries a bearer token in the Authorization header. A token is issued for one project and one environment, and it stops working the moment it is rotated. Access tokens are short lived by design: each one is valid for sixty minutes from the moment it is issued. Long running jobs are expected to renew rather than to hold a single token open, because a held token is the most common cause of a job that works on Monday and fails on Friday.

documents.title: Rejected credentials
documents.text: AUTH-401 is returned whenever the Authorization header is missing, malformed, or carries a token that has already expired. The body names which of the three it was. A malformed header is usually a missing Bearer prefix. An expired token means the sixty minute window closed while the job was still running. A token issued for staging and presented to production also produces AUTH-401, and that one surprises people, because the token itself is perfectly valid.

documents.title: Renewing access
documents.text: A refresh token lives for thirty days and is exchanged for a new access token at the /oauth/renew endpoint. Refresh tokens are single use: the response contains both a new access token and a new refresh token, and the old refresh token is discarded immediately. Storing the refresh token and forgetting to replace it after a renewal is the usual reason a scheduled job runs successfully for weeks and then stops without any change to the code.

documents.title: Request budgets
documents.text: RATE-429 means the project has exceeded its allowance. The default budget is six hundred requests per minute per project, counted across every environment together rather than separately. The response carries a Retry-After header in seconds. Budgets are measured in a sliding window, so a burst of six hundred in one second consumes the entire minute rather than one sixtieth of it.

documents.title: Backing off politely
documents.text: When a call fails with a retryable status the client should wait before trying again, and it should wait longer after each failure. Doubling the pause each time, starting from one second and stopping at sixty, keeps a recovering service from being knocked over by the clients that were waiting for it. Add a small random amount to each pause. Without it, every client that failed at the same moment returns at the same moment.

documents.title: How synchronisation works
documents.text: A sync run compares the records held locally against the records held by the service and transfers only what differs. Each record carries a version counter that increases on every write. The counter, not the content, decides what moves. A full transfer happens only on the first run or after the local store has been discarded.

documents.title: When two writers disagree
documents.text: If the same record is changed in two places between one sync and the next, both changes arrive carrying the same starting version and the service cannot tell which one the user meant. The default behaviour keeps the change that arrived first and returns the second one to the caller untouched, along with the current state of the record, so the caller can decide. Nothing is silently discarded and nothing is silently merged.

documents.title: Synchronisation unavailable
documents.text: SYNC-503 is returned when the synchronisation service is briefly unable to accept work, usually during a regional failover. It is always safe to retry: no partial state is left behind, because a sync run is applied as a single unit or not at all. Sustained SYNC-503 for more than ten minutes is worth reporting rather than retrying.

documents.title: Event delivery
documents.text: Rather than asking repeatedly whether anything has changed, register an endpoint and the service will call it when something does. Delivery is attempted up to eight times over roughly six hours, with the pause growing after each failure. An endpoint that answers with any 2xx status within five seconds is considered to have accepted the event.

documents.title: Proving an event is genuine
documents.text: Each delivered event carries an X-Meridian-Signature header holding a hex digest computed over the raw request body with the project secret. Recompute the digest on the bytes exactly as received, before any JSON parsing, and compare the two using a constant time comparison. Comparing with an ordinary string equality leaks timing information. An event whose digest does not match should be discarded without processing.

documents.title: Walking through long results
documents.text: Collections return at most one hundred items at a time. The response carries a cursor field, and passing it back as the after parameter returns the following page. The cursor encodes a position, not an offset, so records inserted while you are part way through a listing will not cause you to see an item twice or to skip one.

documents.title: Narrowing a listing
documents.text: Listings accept a filter expression over the indexed fields: equality, ranges, and membership in a set. Expressions are combined with and. Filtering happens before pagination, so the cursor walks the filtered collection rather than the whole one. A filter on a field that is not indexed is rejected rather than executed slowly.

documents.title: Writing many records at once
documents.text: Up to five hundred records can be submitted in a single call. The whole submission either succeeds or fails: there is no state in which some of the records were written. A submission that exceeds the limit is rejected rather than truncated. Each record in a submission is validated before any of them is written.

documents.title: Timestamp skew
documents.text: TS-999 means the timestamp on the request differs from the service's own clock by more than five minutes. It is almost never a bug in the caller's code. It is a machine whose clock has drifted, most often a container host or a virtual machine that was suspended and resumed. Enabling a time synchronisation daemon on the host fixes it permanently, where retrying does not.

documents.title: Times and zones
documents.text: Every timestamp accepted or returned is in UTC and carries an explicit offset. Local times are never inferred. A value submitted without an offset is rejected rather than assumed to be UTC, because the assumption is wrong often enough to cause quiet data corruption that is only noticed months later.

documents.title: Where records live
documents.text: A project is created in one region and stays there. Records written to a project never leave the region they were created in, which is what allows the service to make a residency commitment. Choosing a region close to the people using the data also removes most of the latency that is otherwise blamed on the API.

documents.title: Protection of stored data
documents.text: Everything written to disk is encrypted with AES-256 before it is stored, including backups and the audit trail. Keys are held in a separate service and rotated every ninety days; rotation happens without downtime and without re-encrypting existing data, because the key that protects a record is itself protected by the rotating key.

documents.title: Protection of data in flight
documents.text: Connections require TLS 1.3, and plain HTTP requests are refused rather than redirected, because a redirect has already exposed the request. Certificates are issued for ninety days and renewed automatically. Clients that pin a certificate rather than a certificate authority will break at renewal.

documents.title: The record of who did what
documents.text: Every write, every permission change and every token issued is recorded with the actor, the time, and the address the call came from. The trail is append only and cannot be edited through the API. Entries are retained for four hundred days and can be exported.

documents.title: Removing things permanently
documents.text: A deleted record is marked and hidden immediately, then destroyed thirty days later. During that window it can be restored. After it, restoration is genuinely impossible rather than merely difficult, because the record is removed from backups as well.

documents.title: Getting the client library
documents.text: The Python client is installed from PyPI and supports Python 3.10 and above. It reads the token from the MERIDIAN_TOKEN environment variable when one is not passed explicitly. The library retries retryable failures on its own using the backoff described elsewhere, so most callers should not write retry loops of their own.

documents.title: Working from a terminal
documents.text: The command line tool wraps the same operations as the library and is convenient for one-off work and for scripts. It stores credentials in the operating system keychain rather than in a file in the home directory. Output is human readable by default and machine readable with a flag.

documents.title: How much can be stored
documents.text: A project may hold up to ten million records and fifty gigabytes in total. Reaching either limit stops writes but never stops reads, so an application that has run out of room keeps serving its users while somebody fixes it. Usage is reported on the project page and through the API.

documents.title: Limits on a single item
documents.text: One record may not exceed one megabyte once serialised, and one attached file may not exceed one hundred megabytes. Items larger than this are expected to live in object storage with only a reference held here, which is also considerably cheaper.

documents.title: Versions of the interface
documents.text: The interface is versioned by date, and the version is chosen with a header. A project is pinned to the version that was current when it was created, so behaviour does not change underneath an application that is not being actively maintained. Moving to a newer version is an explicit action.

documents.title: Retiring old behaviour
documents.text: A version is supported for at least twenty four months after the next one is published. Notice is given twelve months before anything stops working, and again at three months and at one month. Nothing is ever removed without the full notice period, including behaviour that was clearly a mistake.

documents.title: Sessions in the dashboard
documents.text: A browser session in the dashboard is separate from an API token and lasts twelve hours. Signing out ends the session everywhere, including other tabs, but does not revoke any API token the account has issued. People who expect signing out to stop a running job are usually surprised by this.

documents.title: Accounts that are not people
documents.text: A service account belongs to a project rather than to a person, which means it survives someone leaving the company. It cannot sign in to the dashboard and it cannot own billing. Automated work should always run as one of these rather than under an employee's own credentials.

documents.title: Who may do what
documents.text: Permissions are granted through roles rather than individually. Reader may list and fetch, Writer adds creation and modification, Owner adds deletion and the ability to grant roles to others. A role is always scoped to one project, and there is deliberately no way to grant a permission outside a role.

documents.title: Keys and tokens are different things
documents.text: An API key identifies a project and never expires; a token identifies a session and expires in an hour. Keys are appropriate for server side code you control and inappropriate for anything that ships to a user's device, because a key embedded in a mobile application is a key you have published.

documents.title: Restricting where calls may come from
documents.text: A project can list the network addresses permitted to reach it. A call arriving from anywhere else is refused before the token is even examined, which is why an allowlist mistake looks like an authentication problem without producing an authentication error code.

documents.title: Connection timed out
documents.text: CONN-408 means the request was accepted but the body did not arrive within thirty seconds. It is usually a slow uploader or a proxy buffering the request rather than anything wrong with the payload. Raising the client side timeout does not help, because the limit being reached is the service's own.

documents.title: The payload was not acceptable
documents.text: VALID-422 means the request was understood but the contents failed validation. The body lists every field that failed and why, rather than stopping at the first one, so a single round trip is enough to fix a form. A field that is not in the schema at all is reported as unknown rather than ignored silently.

documents.title: Out of room
documents.text: QUOTA-507 means the project has reached its storage allowance and can no longer accept writes. Reads continue to work. Deleting records frees the space only after the thirty day destruction window has passed, so freeing space is not an immediate remedy and raising the allowance is.

documents.title: Making a retry safe
documents.text: Supply an idempotency key on any call that creates something. If the same key arrives twice the original result is returned rather than a second object being made. Keys are remembered for twenty four hours. Without one, a client that retries after a timeout has no way to know whether the first attempt succeeded.

documents.title: When part of a stream fails
documents.text: A streaming export sends records as they are read. If the connection drops part way through, the records already received are valid and complete; the export simply stopped. Resume by passing the last record identifier you saw rather than starting again from the beginning.

documents.title: Encrypting particular fields
documents.text: Individual fields can be marked so that their contents are encrypted with a key the project supplies rather than the service's own. Such fields can still be fetched but can no longer be filtered on, because the service can no longer read them. This is the trade that surprises people.

documents.title: Looking after keys
documents.text: Keys used for storage encryption are held in a dedicated key service, never on the machines that serve requests, and every use is recorded. A project may supply its own key instead; if it is withdrawn, the data becomes permanently unreadable, which is the point of the feature and also its risk.

documents.title: Pinning certificates
documents.text: Clients that pin a specific certificate rather than the issuing authority will stop working every ninety days when the certificate is renewed. Pin the authority if you must pin something. Most applications should pin nothing and rely on the operating system's trust store.

documents.title: Leaving your network
documents.text: Calls go out to a small, published set of addresses that changes rarely, and the list is available as a machine readable document for firewall rules. Restricting outbound traffic to that list is supported and common in regulated environments.

documents.title: Moving records between places
documents.text: Records cannot be moved from the region a project was created in. Copying them elsewhere means exporting and importing into a new project, and the export is a deliberate, audited action rather than a setting. This is how the residency commitment is kept honest.

documents.title: Copies kept against disaster
documents.text: A full copy is taken nightly and kept for thirty five days, and copies are held in a second location within the same region. Restoring is a support request rather than a button, because a restore replaces live data and that is not something to do by accident.

documents.title: Removing an attached file
documents.text: Deleting a record hides its attached files immediately, but the bytes are removed on the same thirty day schedule as the record itself. A file shared by two records survives until both are gone. There is no way to remove a file while keeping the record that points at it.

documents.title: Putting results in order
documents.text: Listings are ordered by creation time, newest first, unless a sort field is given. Only indexed fields may be sorted on. Sorting is applied before paging, so changing the sort invalidates any cursor you are holding and you must start the listing again.

documents.title: Looking for text inside records
documents.text: Filtering compares a field to a value; searching looks for words inside text fields and ranks what it finds. Searching is available only on fields marked as searchable when the project was set up, and marking a field later requires the existing records to be reindexed.

documents.title: Somewhere to experiment
documents.text: Every project has a second environment with its own data and its own tokens, intended for trying things out. Nothing in it is backed up and everything in it is removed after ninety days of inactivity. A token issued in one environment is refused by the other, which produces an authentication failure that looks puzzling until you notice it.
